claim: DNMT3A is an important facilitator of differentiation of both embryonic and hematopoietic stem cells.
source: DNA Methyltransferase 3 A (DNMT3A) is an important facilitator of differentiation of both embryonic and hematopoietic stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established scientific literature about DNMT3A's role in stem cell differentiation.

claim: Heterozygous germline mutations in DNMT3A lead to Tatton-Brown-Rahman Syndrome (TBRS), characterized by obesity and excessive height.
source: Heterozygous germline mutations in DNMT3A lead to Tatton-Brown-Rahman Syndrome (TBRS), characterized by obesity and excessive height.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical literature describing TBRS phenotypes.

claim: Heterozygous knockout mice recapitulate cardinal TBRS phenotypes.
source: here we investigated a role in adipocyte progenitors utilizing heterozygous knockout mice that recapitulate cardinal TBRS phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing that the mouse model exhibits TBRS-like features.

claim: Heterozygous Dnmt3a knockout mice become morbidly obese due to adipocyte enlargement and tissue expansion.
source: These mice become morbidly obese due to adipocyte enlargement and tissue expansion.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including body weight measurements, DEXA analysis, and histological examination of adipose tissue.

claim: Adipose tissue in heterozygous Dnmt3a knockout mice exhibited defects in preadipocyte maturation.
source: Adipose tissue in these mice exhibited defects in preadipocyte maturation and precocious activation of inflammatory gene networks, including interleukin-6 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data showing altered differentiation trajectories and gene expression patterns.

claim: Adipose tissue in heterozygous Dnmt3a knockout mice exhibited precocious activation of inflammatory gene networks, including interleukin-6 signaling.
source: Adipose tissue in these mice exhibited defects in preadipocyte maturation and precocious activation of inflammatory gene networks, including interleukin-6 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data and flow cytometry showing elevated IL6 expression.

claim: Adipocyte progenitor cell lines lacking DNMT3A exhibited aberrant differentiation.
source: Adipocyte progenitor cell lines lacking DNMT3A exhibited aberrant differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experiments with CRISPR-generated knockout cell lines showing impaired lipogenesis and lipolysis.

claim: Mice in which Dnmt3a was specifically ablated in adipocyte progenitors showed enlarged fat depots and increased progenitor numbers.
source: Furthermore, mice in which Dnmt3a was specifically ablated in adipocyte progenitors showed enlarged fat depots and increased progenitor numbers, partly recapitulating the TBRS obesity phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using Prx-Cre conditional knockout mice showing increased fat mass and progenitor cell numbers.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A led to constitutive DNA hypomethylation in adipocyte progenitors.
source: Loss of DNMT3A led to constitutive DNA hypomethylation, such that the DNA methylation landscape of young adipocyte progenitors resemble that of older wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data showing reduced DNA methylation in DNMT3A-deficient cells.

claim: The DNA methylation landscape of young DNMT3A-deficient adipocyte progenitors resembles that of older wild-type mice.
source: Loss of DNMT3A led to constitutive DNA hypomethylation, such that the DNA methylation landscape of young adipocyte progenitors resemble that of older wild-type mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of DNA methylation patterns across age and genotype.

claim: DNMT3A coordinates both the central and local control of energy storage required to maintain normal weight and prevent inflammatory obesity.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that DNMT3A coordinates both the central and local control of energy storage required to maintain normal weight and prevent inflammatory obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing both hypothalamic effects on feeding behavior and direct effects on adipocyte progenitor function.

claim: Deletion of Dnmt3a in mice results in postnatal lethality.
source: Deletion of Dnmt3a in mice results in postnatal lethality, confirming its necessity during development (Li et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Somatic mutations in DNMT3A are enriched in the hematopoietic system during aging and malignancy.
source: In humans, somatic mutations in DNMT3A are enriched in the hematopoietic system during aging and malignancy (Ley et al., 2010; Tovy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on DNMT3A mutations in hematopoietic disorders.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells alters their epigenetic landscape, increasing the stem cell pool through self-renewal at the expense of differentiation.
source: Loss of DNMT3A in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells alters their epigenetic landscape, increasing the stem cell pool through self-renewal at the expense of differentiation (Challen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on DNMT3A function in hematopoietic stem cells.

claim: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS) is characterized by excessive height in approximately 80% of individuals.
source: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS; OMIM: 615879) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014), a dominant disorder characterized by excessive height (~80% of individuals), intellectual disability (~80% of individuals), and obesity (~70% of individuals) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014; Tatton-Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies describing TBRS phenotypes.

claim: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS) is characterized by intellectual disability in approximately 80% of individuals.
source: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS; OMIM: 615879) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014), a dominant disorder characterized by excessive height (~80% of individuals), intellectual disability (~80% of individuals), and obesity (~70% of individuals) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014; Tatton-Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies describing TBRS phenotypes.

claim: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS) is characterized by obesity in approximately 70% of individuals.
source: Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS; OMIM: 615879) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014), a dominant disorder characterized by excessive height (~80% of individuals), intellectual disability (~80% of individuals), and obesity (~70% of individuals) (Tatton-Brown et al., 2014; Tatton-Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies describing TBRS phenotypes.

claim: Dnmt3a haploinsufficient mice recapitulate key TBRS phenotypes, including enlarged body size and obesity.
source: We and others have recently shown that Dnmt3a haploinsufficent mice can be used to study TBRS (Christian et al., 2020; Tovy et al., 2022). These mice recapitulate key TBRS phenotypes, including enlarged body size and obesity (Christian et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies on Dnmt3a haploinsufficient mouse models.

claim: The mechanisms through which DNMT3A regulates weight gain in TBRS are incompletely understood.
source: However, the mechanisms through which DNMT3A regulates weight gain in TBRS are incompletely understood.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on review of existing literature.

claim: Only a few genes have been identified in which mutations exert causal roles in human obesity.
source: Obesity is a complex energy balance disorder reflecting deficient communication between the hypothalamus and adipose tissue, and only a few genes have so far been identified in which mutations exert causal roles in humans (Choquet and Meyre, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review of genetic causes of obesity.

claim: The majority of genes causing human obesity play a role in the central nervous system.
source: Of these genes, the majority play a role in the central nervous system, which is pivotal in regulating behaviors controlling nutrient update and energy expenditure.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about genetic causes of obesity.

claim: Mechanisms that impact adipocyte progenitor expansion and differentiation can lead to obesity.
source: Yet, although it is well known that mechanisms that impact adipocyte progenitor expansion and differentiation will also lead to obesity, the data on a potential role for DNA methylation in regulating adipose tissue are conflicting (Ma and Kang, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to literature on adipocyte biology and obesity.

claim: Broad inhibition of DNA methyltransferases with 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine promotes lipid accumulation in preadipocyte cell lines.
source: While broad inhibition of DNA methyltransferases with compounds such as 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine was reported to promote lipid accumulation in preadipocyte cell lines (Yang et al., 2016), DNMT inhibition in preadipocyte and mesenchymal precursor cell lines reduced adipogenic differentiation capacity (Chen et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: DNMT inhibition in preadipocyte and mesenchymal precursor cell lines reduced adipogenic differentiation capacity.
source: While broad inhibition of DNA methyltransferases with compounds such as 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine was reported to promote lipid accumulation in preadipocyte cell lines (Yang et al., 2016), DNMT inhibition in preadipocyte and mesenchymal precursor cell lines reduced adipogenic differentiation capacity (Chen et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Homozygous ablation of Dnmt3a specifically in hypothalamic Sim1-positive neurons led to hyperphagia and obesity.
source: While one study showed homozygous ablation of Dnmt3a specifically in hypothalamic Sim1-positive neurons led to hyperphagia and obesity (Kohno et al., 2014), knockout of Dnmt3a in mature adipocytes protected mice from developing insulin resistance while on a high-fat-diet (You et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: Knockout of Dnmt3a in mature adipocytes protected mice from developing insulin resistance while on a high-fat-diet.
source: While one study showed homozygous ablation of Dnmt3a specifically in hypothalamic Sim1-positive neurons led to hyperphagia and obesity (Kohno et al., 2014), knockout of Dnmt3a in mature adipocytes protected mice from developing insulin resistance while on a high-fat-diet (You et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published experimental studies.

claim: DNMT3A regulates adipose stem and progenitor cell function.
source: Our results establish that DNMT3A directly regulates obesity through the adipose tissue, in addition to its role in the hypothalamus, and demonstrate how constitutive loss of DNMT3A creates a domino effect in which excess feeding together with faulty adipocytes lead to obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the manuscript showing effects on adipocyte progenitors.

claim: DNMT3A directly regulates obesity through the adipose tissue, in addition to its role in the hypothalamus.
source: Our results establish that DNMT3A directly regulates obesity through the adipose tissue, in addition to its role in the hypothalamus, and demonstrate how constitutive loss of DNMT3A creates a domino effect in which excess feeding together with faulty adipocytes lead to obesity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing both central and peripheral effects of DNMT3A loss.

claim: Constitutive loss of DNMT3A creates a domino effect in which excess feeding together with faulty adipocytes lead to obesity.
source: Our results establish that DNMT3A directly regulates obesity through the adipose tissue, in addition to its role in the hypothalamus, and demonstrate how constitutive loss of DNMT3A creates a domino effect in which excess feeding together with faulty adipocytes lead to obesity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined experimental findings showing both increased food intake and adipocyte dysfunction.

claim: WT and 3A-HET mice were indistinguishable until around 3 months of age.
source: In humans, TBRS phenotypes become particularly evident around adolescence when patients exhibit marked height and weight gain (Tatton-Brown et al., 2018). Similarly, WT and 3A-HET mice were indistinguishable until around 3 months of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant differences in early measurements.

claim: By 6 months, both male and female 3A-HET mice were heavier than controls.
source: However, by 6 months, both male and female 3A-HET mice were heavier than controls (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At 12 months of age, the cohort of HET mice averaged 3 standard deviations above the mean weight of WT mice, becoming obese.
source: At 12 months of age, the cohort of HET averaged 3 standard deviations (SD) above the mean weight of WT mice, becoming obese (Figure 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight distribution data shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: The increased length of 3A-HET mice was mild and could not account for the increased weight.
source: The increased length of 3A-HET mice, while statistically significant, was mild, and therefore could not account for the increased weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by length measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and inference about the relationship between length and weight.

claim: 3A-HET mice showed a steady increase in fat percentage and a concomitant reduction in lean mass.
source: We detected a steady increase in fat percentage and a concomitant reduction in lean mass in 3A-HET mice (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA analysis data shown in Figure 1C, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Adipose tissue can expand through either increased number of adipocyte cells (hyperplasia) or increased adipocyte cell size (hypertrophy).
source: Adipose tissue can expand through either increased number of adipocyte cells due to proliferation and differentiation of adipocyte precursors (hyperplasia) or increased adipocyte cell size (hypertrophy).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about mechanisms of adipose tissue expansion.

claim: White adipose tissue (WAT) functions primarily to store energy.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) functions primarily to store energy, while brown adipose tissue (BAT) performs thermogenic functions.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about adipose tissue biology.

claim: Brown adipose tissue (BAT) performs thermogenic functions.
source: White adipose tissue (WAT) functions primarily to store energy, while brown adipose tissue (BAT) performs thermogenic functions.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about adipose tissue biology.

claim: 3A-HET mice had heavier fat depots across all measured depots at 1 year of age.
source: On average, 3A-HET mice had heavier fat depots across all measured depots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and larger adipocytes in both WAT and BAT depots compared to WT littermates (Figure 1E, F), suggesting the increase in total fat is largely due to hypertrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by fat depot weight measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: 3A-HET mice had larger adipocytes in both WAT and BAT depots compared to WT littermates at 1 year of age.
source: On average, 3A-HET mice had heavier fat depots across all measured depots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and larger adipocytes in both WAT and BAT depots compared to WT littermates (Figure 1E, F), suggesting the increase in total fat is largely due to hypertrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and morphometric measurements shown in Figure 1E, F.

claim: The increase in total fat in 3A-HET mice is largely due to hypertrophy.
source: On average, 3A-HET mice had heavier fat depots across all measured depots (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H) and larger adipocytes in both WAT and BAT depots compared to WT littermates (Figure 1E, F), suggesting the increase in total fat is largely due to hypertrophy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of larger adipocytes rather than increased cell numbers.

claim: Expansion of adipocytes is often accompanied by infiltration of macrophages (CD45+, F4/80+ cells).
source: Expansion of adipocytes is often accompanied by infiltration of macrophages (CD45 +, F4\80 + cells) and indeed we measured more F4/80 cells in WAT from HET mice compared to WT mice at 1 year of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about adipose tissue inflammation.

claim: 3A-HET mice had more F4/80 cells in WAT compared to WT mice at 1 year of age.
source: Expansion of adipocytes is often accompanied by infiltration of macrophages (CD45 +, F4\80 + cells) and indeed we measured more F4/80 cells in WAT from HET mice compared to WT mice at 1 year of age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Reduced DNMT3A leads to pathological adipose expansion and spontaneous obesity.
source: These results suggest that reduced DNMT3A leads to pathological adipose expansion and spontaneous obesity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined experimental findings on adipose tissue expansion and obesity development.

claim: Fatty liver is strongly associated with obesity.
source: Fatty liver is strongly associated with obesity, we therefore performed histological analysis of WT and 3A-HET mice livers at 1 year of age.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the relationship between obesity and fatty liver.

claim: 3A-HET mice show increased fat accumulation in livers at 1 year of age.
source: We observe increase in fat accumulation in 3A-HET livers, as measured by fat-soluble dye (Oil-Red-O staining).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis with Oil-Red-O staining shown in Figure 1G, H.

claim: Germline loss of DNMT3A leads to weight gain through expansion of adipose tissue and accumulation of lipids in non-adipose tissues such as the liver.
source: Therefore, these results demonstrate that germline loss of DNMT3A leads to weight gain through expansion of adipose tissue, as well as accumulation of lipids in non-adipose tissues such as the liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by combined data on adipose tissue expansion and liver fat accumulation.

claim: Data from heterozygous Dnmt3a KO mice mirror the findings in TBRS patients of increased size and marked obesity that develops after adolescence.
source: Together these data from heterozygous Dnmt3a KO mice mirror the findings in TBRS patients of increased size and marked obesity that develops after adolescence.
evidence: This claim is an inference comparing the mouse model phenotypes to human TBRS phenotypes.

claim: 3A-HET mice showed increased food intake mostly during the dark phase.
source: We measured increased food intake in HET mice mostly during the dark phase (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLAMS data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: HET mice showed a mild change in activity during light phase.
source: HET mice also showed a mild change in activity during light phase and decrease in energy balance calculated by calorie consumption compared to calorie expenditure (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLAMS activity data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: HET mice showed a decrease in energy balance calculated by calorie consumption compared to calorie expenditure.
source: HET mice also showed a mild change in activity during light phase and decrease in energy balance calculated by calorie consumption compared to calorie expenditure (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CLAMS energy balance data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D.

claim: Leptin secreted from adipocytes normally signals satiety to the hypothalamus to restrict food intake and inhibit weight gain.
source: As leptin secreted from adipocytes normally signals satiety to the hypothalamus to restrict food intake and inhibit weight gain (Badman and Flier, 2007; Rosen and Spiegelman, 2014), we measured leptin levels in 3A-HET compared to WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on leptin function.

claim: 3A-HET mice showed a persistent increase in leptin levels compared to WT littermates.
source: We observed a persistent increase in leptin levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G) in mice lacking DNMT3A compared to their WT littermates.
evidence: This claim is supported by leptin measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Heterozygous germline loss of Dnmt3a impacts feeding behavior similarly to homozygous loss of Dnmt3a specifically in the hypothalamus.
source: These data demonstrate that heterozygous germline loss of Dnmt3a impacts feeding behavior similarly to homozygous loss of Dnmt3a specifically in the hypothalamus (Kohno et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is an inference comparing the current findings to published data on hypothalamic Dnmt3a knockout.

claim: Prolonged weight gain can result in insulin resistance, which manifests as hyperinsulinemia combined with hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia.
source: Prolonged weight gain can result in insulin resistance, which manifests as hyperinsulinemia combined with hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the metabolic consequences of obesity.

claim: At 2 months, WT and HET mice did not display major differences in fasting glucose and insulin levels or when challenged with a glucose tolerance test.
source: At 2 months, WT and HET mice did not display major differences in fasting glucose and insulin levels or when challenged with a glucose tolerance test (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose and insulin measurements and glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2C–E.

claim: At 6 months, 3A-HET mice had higher fasting levels of glucose and insulin.
source: However, at 6 months, when 3A-HET mice are statistically heavier than WT, they had higher fasting levels of glucose and insulin (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose and insulin measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: At 10 months, HET mice develop profound glucose and insulin resistance.
source: Further, at 10 months HET mice develop profound glucose and insulin resistance (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of a Dnmt3a allele in this mouse model of TBRS leads to obesity and contributes to insulin resistance at older ages.
source: These results establish that loss of a Dnmt3a in this mouse model of TBRS leads to obesity and contributes to insulin resistance at older ages.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined metabolic phenotyping data.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A can inhibit somatic stem cell differentiation.
source: Because loss of DNMT3A can inhibit somatic stem cell differentiation (Challen et al., 2011), we scrutinized adipocyte maturation in 3A-HET mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on DNMT3A function in stem cells.

claim: Adipose tissue depots are composed of multiple cell populations including preadipocyte stem and progenitor cells, preadipocytes, and fully mature adipocytes, which change during development.
source: Adipose tissue depots are composed of multiple cell populations including preadipocyte stem and progenitor cells, preadipocytes, and fully mature adipocytes, which change during development (Merrick et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on adipose tissue cellular composition.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing was performed on cells isolated from inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) of WT and 3A-HET mice at 8 weeks and 1 year old.
source: To examine how loss of Dnmt3a affected these cell populations, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) on cells isolated from inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) of WT and 3A-HET mice at 8 weeks and 1 year old.
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of gene expression of all cells obtained six clusters.
source: To define component cell types, we next performed unsupervised clustering of gene expression of all cells and obtained six clusters (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cluster 1 expressed key genes associated with committed preadipocytes, adipocyte differentiation, and inflammatory activation such as Fabp4, Lpl, and Icam1.
source: Cluster 1 expressed key genes associated with committed preadipocytes, adipocyte differentiation, and inflammatory activation such as fatty acid binding protein (Fabp4), lipoprotein lipase (Lpl), and intercellular adhesion molecule–1 (Icam1) (Balamurugan and Sterneck, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis and citation to literature on these markers.

claim: Cluster 2 displayed markers of committed differentiating preadipocytes (Fabp4, Lpl, and Plin2), as well as enrichment for the tissue factor F3.
source: Cluster 2 displayed markers of committed differentiating preadipocytes (Fabp4, Lpl, and Plin2), as well as enrichment for the tissue factor F3, a marker of adipogenesis-regulatory cells associated with adipocyte differentiation (Schwalie et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis and citation to literature on F3 as a marker.

claim: F3 is a marker of adipogenesis-regulatory cells associated with adipocyte differentiation.
source: Cluster 2 displayed markers of committed differentiating preadipocytes (Fabp4, Lpl, and Plin2), as well as enrichment for the tissue factor F3, a marker of adipogenesis-regulatory cells associated with adipocyte differentiation (Schwalie et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on F3 function.

claim: Clusters 3 and 4 expressed a mix of stem and progenitor markers (Dpp4, Cd34) and adipocyte markers (Fabp4, Lpl), indicating they contained cells in transition.
source: We observed that both clusters 3 and 4 expressed a mix of stem and progenitor markers (Dpp4, Cd34) and adipocyte markers (Fabp4, Lpl), indicating they contained cells in transition.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis and inference about cell state based on marker expression.

claim: Dpp4 is a marker of multipotent progenitors within iWAT with some attributes of mesenchymal stem cells.
source: Importantly, dipeptidyl peptidase (Dpp4) is a marker of multipotent progenitors within iWAT with some attributes of mesenchymal stem cells (Merrick et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on Dpp4 as a marker.

claim: Cluster 3 uniquely had increased expression of pro-inflammatory markers.
source: However, cluster 3 uniquely had increased expression of pro-inflammatory markers.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3C, D.

claim: Clusters 5 and 6 harbored gene profiles of multipotent stem and progenitor cells (Dpp4, Cd34, Ly6a, and Pi16) and did not express differentiated adipocyte markers such as Fabp4.
source: Clusters 5 and 6 harbored gene profiles of multipotent stem and progenitor cells (Dpp4, Cd34, Ly6a (encoding Sca-1), and Pi16) and did not express differentiated adipocyte markers such as Fabp4; most of these markers displayed higher expression in cluster 5 than cluster 6 (Figure 3B, C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3B, C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Three major groups of cells were classified: committed preadipocytes (COM; clusters 1–2, with high Fabp4), primed preadipocytes (PRI; clusters 3–4, with both stem-like and differentiation markers), and stem and progenitor clusters (ST; clusters 5–6).
source: With these data and the gradient in Dpp4 and Fabp4 expression across clusters (Figure 3E), we classified three major groups of cells: committed preadipocytes (COM; clusters 1–2, with high Fabp4), primed preadipocytes PRI; (clusters 3–4, with both stem-like and differentiation markers), and stem and progenitor clusters (ST; clusters 5–6).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of gene expression patterns to define cell states.

claim: At young ages, the proportions of stem and primed preadipocyte progenitors were higher in 3A-HET mice compared to WT.
source: We found that at young ages, the proportions of stem and primed preadipocytes progenitors were higher in 3A-HET mice (1.35- and 1.5-fold, respectively) compared to WT, while the proportion of cells in the committed clusters was lower than in WT (1.4- fold) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cell proportions shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: At young ages, the proportion of cells in the committed clusters was lower in 3A-HET mice than in WT.
source: We found that at young ages, the proportions of stem and primed preadipocytes progenitors were higher in 3A-HET mice (1.35- and 1.5-fold, respectively) compared to WT, while the proportion of cells in the committed clusters was lower than in WT (1.4- fold) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cell proportions shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Young 3A-HET mice harbor a larger pool of stem and progenitor cells at the expense of committed adipocytes.
source: These differences in the stem and progenitor-primed clusters indicate that young 3A-HET mice harbor a larger pool of stem and progenitor cells at the expense of committed adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cell proportion data.

claim: After 1 year, cells in committed clusters decreased proportionally in WT but increased in 3A-HET iWAT.
source: After 1 year, when 3A-HET mice are obese, cells in committed clusters decreased proportionally in WT but increased in 3A-HET iWAT (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cell proportions over time shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A decrease in the ST stem cluster was detected in 1-year-old 3A-HET compared to WT mice.
source: In addition, we detected a decrease in the ST stem cluster in 1-year-old 3A-HET compared to WT mice, suggesting that adipose expansion in HET mice ultimately results in a decrease in the stem and progenitor clusters, possibly due to exhaustion or increased proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of cell proportions shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Adipose expansion in HET mice ultimately results in a decrease in the stem and progenitor clusters, possibly due to exhaustion or increased proliferation.
source: In addition, we detected a decrease in the ST stem cluster in 1-year-old 3A-HET compared to WT mice, suggesting that adipose expansion in HET mice ultimately results in a decrease in the stem and progenitor clusters, possibly due to exhaustion or increased proliferation.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in stem cell proportions.

claim: Preadipocyte cells were more abundant in 3A-HET mice at 8 weeks relative to WT.
source: Consistent with our scRNAseq data, we found that, though preadipocyte cells were more abundant in 3A-HET mice at 8 weeks relative to WT, by 1 year their numbers decreased relative to WT (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: By 1 year, preadipocyte cell numbers in 3A-HET mice decreased relative to WT.
source: Consistent with our scRNAseq data, we found that, though preadipocyte cells were more abundant in 3A-HET mice at 8 weeks relative to WT, by 1 year their numbers decreased relative to WT (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry quantification shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Intermediate stem and primed adipocytes are the primary source for adipose tissue expansion in WT mice.
source: These results imply that intermediate stem and primed adipocytes are the primary source for adipose tissue expansion in WT mice, while in 3A-HET mice, increased energy intake and hyperphagia continuously require more preadipocyte progenitors, ultimately resulting in depletion of stem cells.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cell proportion changes over time.

claim: In 3A-HET mice, increased energy intake and hyperphagia continuously require more preadipocyte progenitors, ultimately resulting in depletion of stem cells.
source: These results imply that intermediate stem and primed adipocytes are the primary source for adipose tissue expansion in WT mice, while in 3A-HET mice, increased energy intake and hyperphagia continuously require more preadipocyte progenitors, ultimately resulting in depletion of stem cells.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation combining feeding behavior data with cell proportion changes.

claim: Pseudotime analysis revealed two major trajectories (A and B), with cluster 5 representing the most naïve position.
source: This analysis revealed two major trajectories (A and B), with cluster 5 representing the most naïve position (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Trajectory A included stem-like cluster 6, primed cluster 4, and committed preadipocytes cluster 2.
source: Trajectory A included stem-like cluster 6, and primed (cluster 4) and committed preadipocytes (cluster 2, Fabp4high).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Trajectory B passed through clusters that displayed hallmarks of the inflammatory response including upregulated Il6 and Ccl2.
source: Trajectory B passed through clusters that displayed hallmarks of the inflammatory response including upregulated interleukin 6 (Il6) and Ccl2 (C-C motif chemokine ligand 2) (Figure 3B and 6C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Trajectory B included the pro-inflammatory primed cluster 3 ending in committed preadipocytes cluster 1.
source: Trajectory B also included the pro-inflammatory primed (cluster 3) ending in committed preadipocytes (cluster 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by pseudotime trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Young WT cells were weighted toward trajectory A.
source: Young WT cells were weighted toward trajectory A, while young 3A-HET cells were much more heavily represented along the pro-inflammatory B trajectory, with more cells retaining stem-like and primed preadipocyte phenotypes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Young 3A-HET cells were much more heavily represented along the pro-inflammatory B trajectory.
source: Young WT cells were weighted toward trajectory A, while young 3A-HET cells were much more heavily represented along the pro-inflammatory B trajectory, with more cells retaining stem-like and primed preadipocyte phenotypes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At 8 weeks of age, WT and 3A-HET mice did not display overt differences in adiposity.
source: Importantly, at 8 weeks of age, WT and 3A-HET mice did not display overt differences in adiposity, indicating these cell-state differences precede the phenotypic alterations.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight and composition data showing no significant differences at 8 weeks.

claim: Cell-state differences in 3A-HET mice precede the phenotypic alterations in adiposity.
source: Importantly, at 8 weeks of age, WT and 3A-HET mice did not display overt differences in adiposity, indicating these cell-state differences precede the phenotypic alterations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation of molecular changes before phenotypic changes.

claim: After 1 year, WT mice showed more cells in the pro-inflammatory path, consistent with the known inflammatory effects of aging in adipose tissue.
source: Examining the trajectories after 1 year, we noted in WT mice more cells in the pro-inflammatory path, consistent with the known inflammatory effects of aging in adipose tissue (Tchkonia et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis and citation to literature on adipose tissue aging.

claim: After 1 year, 3A-HET preadipocytes showed a particularly strong bias toward pro-inflammatory trajectory B.
source: Strikingly, the 3A-HET preadipocytes showed a particularly strong bias toward pro-inflammatory trajectory B (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cluster 5 serves as a source for both pathways.
source: Altogether, these analyses suggest that cluster 5 serves a source for both pathways, and 3A-HET adipose tissue, even at a young age, displays a bias towards an inflammatory state, which becomes exacerbated in aging obese preadipocytes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the pseudotime trajectory analysis.

claim: 3A-HET adipose tissue, even at a young age, displays a bias towards an inflammatory state, which becomes exacerbated in aging obese preadipocytes.
source: Altogether, these analyses suggest that cluster 5 serves a source for both pathways, and 3A-HET adipose tissue, even at a young age, displays a bias towards an inflammatory state, which becomes exacerbated in aging obese preadipocytes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the trajectory analysis over time.

claim: The inflammatory state of adipose tissue correlates strongly with insulin resistance and other co-morbidities of obesity.
source: Because the inflammatory state of adipose tissue correlates strongly with insulin resistance and other co-morbidities of obesity, we examined the inflammatory markers and trajectories more closely.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the relationship between adipose inflammation and metabolic disease.

claim: 3A-HET cells were primed to express higher pro-inflammatory marker genes in the transient and committed preadipocytes groups.
source: Differential gene expression analysis supported our observation that 3A-HET cells were primed to express higher pro-inflammatory marker genes in the transient and committed preadipocytes groups (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: 3A-HET preadipocytes displayed activation of inflammatory signaling in the IL6 and interferon gamma signaling pathways even in the stem-like cells.
source: Moreover, 3A-HET preadipocytes displayed activation of inflammatory signaling in the IL6 and interferon gamma signaling pathways even in the stem-like cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IL6 was markedly elevated in 3A-HET preadipocytes at 6 months of age.
source: To verify that IL6 was upregulated, we performed intracellular flow cytometry analysis of preadipocytes from WT and 3A-HET mice (6 months of age), confirming markedly elevated IL6 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Genes representing full differentiation of adipocytes (Apoe, Lpl, Fabp4, and Igfbp3) were expressed at lower levels in 3A-HET cells in the primed and committed cell clusters relative to WT tissue at both time points.
source: Along with the 3A-HET inflammatory phenotype, genes representing full differentiation of adipocytes (Apoe, Lpl, Fabp4, and Igfbp3) were expressed at lower levels in 3A-HET cells in the primed and committed cell clusters relative to that of WT tissue at both time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: WT cells displayed an epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) signature only in the stem cell clusters.
source: In addition, unlike WT cells which displayed an epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) signature only in the stem cell clusters, 3A-HET tissue displayed enrichment of stem-like EMT even in the primed and committed clusters, suggesting a failure to suppress the stem cell program in 3A-HET preadipocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 3A-HET tissue displayed enrichment of stem-like EMT even in the primed and committed clusters.
source: In addition, unlike WT cells which displayed an epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) signature only in the stem cell clusters, 3A-HET tissue displayed enrichment of stem-like EMT even in the primed and committed clusters, suggesting a failure to suppress the stem cell program in 3A-HET preadipocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There is a failure to suppress the stem cell program in 3A-HET preadipocytes.
source: In addition, unlike WT cells which displayed an epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT) signature only in the stem cell clusters, 3A-HET tissue displayed enrichment of stem-like EMT even in the primed and committed clusters, suggesting a failure to suppress the stem cell program in 3A-HET preadipocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the EMT signature persistence in differentiated cells.

claim: DNMT3A plays a role in adipocyte precursor cell differentiation and maturation.
source: Together, these results support a role for DNMT3A in adipocyte precursor cell differentiation and maturation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined gene expression and trajectory analysis data.

claim: Heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a in preadipocytes promotes pro-inflammatory obesity.
source: Our data also indicate that even heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a in preadipocytes promotes pro-inflammatory obesity.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined phenotypic and molecular data.

claim: Dnmt3a-knockout clonal cell lines were generated in established white (3T3-L1) and brown (BAC-C4) preadipocyte models.
source: Therefore, we generated Dnmt3a-knockout (KO) clonal cell lines in established white (3T3-L1) and brown (BAC-C4) preadipocyte models (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 3).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental approach and is supported by Western blot validation shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Both 3T3-KO and BAC-KO cell lines exhibited higher proliferation rates than controls.
source: In both lineages, Dnmt3a-KO clones exhibited higher proliferation rates than controls (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), mirroring the expansion of 3A-HET progenitor cells in our scRNAseq analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All four cell lines (3T3-Con, 3T3-KO, BAC-Con, BAC-KO) differentiated and formed mature adipocytes that stored lipids.
source: We found that all four lines differentiated and formed mature adipocytes that stored lipids, but both 3T3-KO and BAC-KO stored fewer lipids (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipid staining data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both 3T3-KO and BAC-KO cell lines stored fewer lipids than controls.
source: We found that all four lines differentiated and formed mature adipocytes that stored lipids, but both 3T3-KO and BAC-KO stored fewer lipids (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipid staining and quantification shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both KO cell lines accumulated fewer lipid droplets when challenged with exogenous fluorescent fatty acids.
source: In addition, both KO cell lines accumulated fewer lipid droplets when challenged with exogenous fluorescent fatty acids, indicating that loss of DNMT3A impairs lipogenesis (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescent fatty acid uptake assays shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A impairs lipogenesis.
source: In addition, both KO cell lines accumulated fewer lipid droplets when challenged with exogenous fluorescent fatty acids, indicating that loss of DNMT3A impairs lipogenesis (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the reduced lipid accumulation in knockout cells.

claim: Both KO lineages showed slowed release of fatty acids in response to isoproterenol treatment.
source: We observed slowed release of fatty acids in both KO lineages with no effect on cell numbers (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Phosphorylation of hormone sensitive lipase (HSL) was significantly reduced in both KO lineages.
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of the key lipase regulator hormone sensitive lipase (HSL) was significantly reduced in both KO lineages (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), consistent with reduced lipolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A in preadipocytes allows at least partial differentiation but impairs both lipogenesis and lipolysis responses in WAT and BAT.
source: Combined, these results indicate loss of DNMT3A in preadipocytes allows at least partial differentiation but impairs both lipogenesis and lipolysis responses in WAT and BAT.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined functional assay data from cell lines.

claim: Approximately 1000 genes were significantly differentially expressed between BAC-Con and BAC-KO cells following differentiation.
source: We identified ~1000 genes that were significantly differentially expressed between BAC-Con and BAC-KO cells following differentiation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: 30% of genes upregulated in KO compared to control following differentiation or ISO treatment were already differentially expressed in non-treated cells.
source: When we classified genes upregulated in KO compared to control following differentiation or ISO treatment, we noticed that 30% (244 genes, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G left) were already differentially expressed in NT cells (Figure 3G top).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Only a small number (41 genes) of genes that were upregulated in control cells following differentiation were already altered at baseline in KO cells.
source: In contrast, only a small number (41 genes, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G right) of genes that were upregulated in control cells following differentiation were already altered at baseline in KO cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: DNMT3A is needed for gene repression during adipocyte differentiation.
source: The large number of genes not downregulated in KO cells during differentiation indicates that DNMT3A is needed for gene repression during adipocyte differentiation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the gene expression patterns in knockout cells.

claim: Genes upregulated in control cells during differentiation were enriched for adipogenesis.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis showed that while genes upregulated in control cells during differentiation were enriched for adipogenesis, KO cells displayed enrichment for EMT and inflammation (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: KO cells displayed enrichment for EMT and inflammation.
source: Pathway enrichment analysis showed that while genes upregulated in control cells during differentiation were enriched for adipogenesis, KO cells displayed enrichment for EMT and inflammation (Figure 5G, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Genes upregulated in BAC-KO significantly overlapped with those in 3T3-L1 siRNA-Dnmt3a (163 genes).
source: Genes upregulated in BAC-KO significantly overlapped with those in 3T3-L1 siRNA-Dnmt3a (163 genes, Figure 5—figure supplement 1H top).
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis comparing datasets shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Pathway enrichment of overlapping genes differentially expressed due to Dnmt3a loss in BAC indicated congruence with the 3T3-L1 cell line, including upregulation of EMT and inflammation.
source: Pathway enrichment of overlapping genes differentially expressed due to Dnmt3a loss in BAC also indicated congruence with in the 3T3-L1 cell line, including upregulation of EMT and inflammation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H bottom; Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The EMT gene signature is consistent with a mesenchymal stem cell state.
source: The EMT gene signature is consistent with a mesenchymal stem cell state, indicating that loss of DNMT3A causes both BAT and WAT to retain a preadipocyte-like gene expression pattern despite at least partial induction of differentiation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on established knowledge about EMT and stem cell states.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A causes both BAT and WAT to retain a preadipocyte-like gene expression pattern despite at least partial induction of differentiation.
source: The EMT gene signature is consistent with a mesenchymal stem cell state, indicating that loss of DNMT3A causes both BAT and WAT to retain a preadipocyte-like gene expression pattern despite at least partial induction of differentiation.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the gene expression patterns in knockout cells.

claim: DNMT3A has a cell-autonomous role in maturation of both white and brown adipocytes.
source: These data establish a cell-autonomous role for DNMT3A in maturation of both white and brown adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the cell line experiments showing direct effects of DNMT3A loss.

claim: Key gene hallmarks differentially expressed in the preadipocyte cell lines (BAC and 3T3) include gene sets identified in the single cell data, such as inflammatory, IL6 and epithelial mesenchymal transition.
source: Our results show that key gene hallmarks differentially expressed in the preadipocyte cell lines (BAC and 3T3) include gene sets identified in our single cell data, such as inflammatory, IL6 and epithelial mesenchymal transition (Figure 6A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of in vitro and in vivo data shown in Figure 6A, B.

claim: Expression of inflammatory, IL6, and EMT gene pathways is consistent with incomplete differentiation and upregulation of inflammation following loss of DNMT3A both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Expression of these gene pathways is consistent with incomplete differentiation and upregulation of inflammation following loss of DNMT3A both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the convergent findings from cell lines and mouse models.

claim: 3A-HET mice had less free fatty acids (FFA) in plasma after 12 hr fasting compared to WT.
source: We detected less FFA and glycerol in the plasma in 3A-HET mice compared to WT (~2 fold; Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by FFA measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: 3A-HET mice had less glycerol in plasma after 12 hr fasting compared to WT.
source: We detected less FFA and glycerol in the plasma in 3A-HET mice compared to WT (~2 fold; Figure 6C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by glycerol measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 3A-HET tissues displayed lower secretion of FFA from both BAT and WAT (gonadal, gWAT) compared to WT following ex vivo ISO treatment.
source: 3A-HET tissues displayed lower secretion of FFA from both BAT and WAT (gonadal, gWAT) compared to WT (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3A-HET WAT and BAT tissues released less glycerol compared to WT following ex vivo ISO treatment.
source: In addition, 3A-HET WAT and BAT tissues released less glycerol compared to WT (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 3A-HET fat depots showed diminished activation of p-HSL compared to WT in response to ISO or fasting.
source: Consistent with our in vitro data, western blot analysis of 3A-HET fat depots showed diminished activation of p-HSL compared to WT in response to ISO or fasting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a in vivo reduces lipolytic capacity and subsequent FFA release.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that, similar to homozygous loss of Dnmt3a in cell lines, heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a in vivo reduces lipolytic capacity and subsequent FFA release.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined in vitro and in vivo lipolysis data.

claim: Prx is expressed in the uncommitted mesenchymal progenitors of subcutaneous inguinal fat.
source: Prx is expressed in the uncommitted mesenchymal progenitors of subcutaneous inguinal fat, which were the focus of the analyses described above (Eguchi et al., 2011; Logan et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on Prx expression.

claim: PRX-D3A mice showed a steady yet mild increase in weight (~14%), which became statistically significant at 8 months.
source: We observed a steady yet mild increase in weight (~14%), which became statistically significant at 8 months in PRX-D3A mice (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: PRX-D3A mice displayed elevated fat mass compared to controls.
source: Body composition analysis confirmed that PRX-D3A mice displayed elevated fat mass compared to controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DEXA analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PRX-D3A mice had larger adipocytes in the subcutaneous inguinal fat where Dnmt3a is ablated.
source: In addition, like HET mice, PRX-D3A mice also displayed larger adipocytes in the subcutaneous inguinal fat in which Dnmt3a is ablated, while maintaining similar adipocyte size in gonadal fat in which the Prx-Cre is not expressed (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: PRX-D3A mice maintained similar adipocyte size in gonadal fat where Prx-Cre is not expressed.
source: In addition, like HET mice, PRX-D3A mice also displayed larger adipocytes in the subcutaneous inguinal fat in which Dnmt3a is ablated, while maintaining similar adipocyte size in gonadal fat in which the Prx-Cre is not expressed (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis showing tissue-specific effects.

claim: PRX-D3A mice showed an increase in plasma leptin.
source: Consistent with expansion of adipose tissue in these mice, we also detected an increase in plasma leptin in PRX-D3A mice (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by leptin measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Loss of DNMT3A specifically from adipocyte progenitors contributes to expansion of adipose tissue mass.
source: These results support our hypothesis that loss of DNMT3A specifically from adipocyte progenitors contributes to expansion of adipose tissue mass.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the PRX-D3A mouse phenotype data.

claim: PRX-D3A mice showed a significant increase in the percentage of Sca1+ preadipocyte progenitors only from the subcutaneous inguinal fat.
source: We performed flow cytometry analysis of SVCs extracted from fat pads of subcutaneous inguinal and visceral fat and indeed observed a significant increase in the percentage of Sca1 +preadipocytes progenitors only from the subcutaneous inguinal fat, supporting cell autonomous expansion of adipose progenitors with loss of DNMT3A (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The tissue-specific increase in progenitors supports cell autonomous expansion of adipose progenitors with loss of DNMT3A.
source: We performed flow cytometry analysis of SVCs extracted from fat pads of subcutaneous inguinal and visceral fat and indeed observed a significant increase in the percentage of Sca1 +preadipocytes progenitors only from the subcutaneous inguinal fat, supporting cell autonomous expansion of adipose progenitors with loss of DNMT3A (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the tissue-specific effects in the conditional knockout model.

claim: PRX-D3A subcutaneous inguinal fat showed a decrease in the release of FAA following ex vivo ISO treatment.
source: We also measured the efficacy of lipolysis in subcutaneous inguinal fat from PRX-D3A mice. Similarly to our results from D3A-HET mice, we observed a decrease in the release of FAA from the PRX-D3A fat pads (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo lipolysis assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: DNMT3A regulates obesity via early stages of adipogenesis.
source: Taken together, these results confirm a role for DNMT3A in regulation of obesity via early stages of adipogenesis.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined data from conditional knockout experiments.

claim: In 3A-HET cells, there was a mild (2–4%) yet significant decrease in global methylation compared to WT cells at both time points.
source: In 3A-HET cells, we observed a mild (2–4%) yet significant (p<10–15) decrease in global methylation compared to WT cells in both time points (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Approximately 1100 regions were hypomethylated with age in WT cells (hypo-DMRA).
source: We first determined DNA methylation changes in WT between the two time points, identifying ~1100 regions that were hypomethylated (hypo-DMRA, see methods), and ~2800 regions hypermethylated with age (hyper-DMRA, see methods) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, Figure 8—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGBS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Approximately 2800 regions were hypermethylated with age in WT cells (hyper-DMRA).
source: We first determined DNA methylation changes in WT between the two time points, identifying ~1100 regions that were hypomethylated (hypo-DMRA, see methods), and ~2800 regions hypermethylated with age (hyper-DMRA, see methods) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, Figure 8—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by WGBS analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: WT hypo-DMRA regions tended to be hypomethylated in 3A-HET cells regardless of age.
source: Remarkably, these regions tended to be hypomethylated in 3A-HET cells regardless of age (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Approximately 900 (70%) of WT hypo-DMRA regions displayed lower methylation values (≥19%) in HET cells than WT and most remained hypomethylated at 1 year.
source: Comparing the mean methylation for these regions between young WT and HET cells showed that ~900 of them (70%) displayed lower methylation values (≥19%, blue peak in Figure 8C) in HET cells than WT and most remained hypomethylated at 1 year (Figure 8D and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 8C, D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 3A-HET cells lacking one allele of Dnmt3a began with lower DNA methylation and failed to experience the dynamic methylation changes typically seen in WT cells with age.
source: Therefore, 3A-HET cells lacking one allele of Dnmt3a began with lower DNA methylation and failed to experience the dynamic methylation changes typically seen in WT cells with age.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the DNA methylation dynamics over time.

claim: Young 3A-HET cells displayed significantly lower methylation levels than WT at WT hyper-DMRA regions.
source: When we plotted their mean methylation in 3A-HET cells, young cells displayed significantly lower methylation levels than WT, and methylation was generally even lower at 1 year (~1500, 54%).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 8F.

claim: DNMT3A has a major role in methylation of ageing DMRA regions over time.
source: These data suggest that DNMT3A has a major role in methylation of ageing DMRA regions over time (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the failure to gain methylation in DNMT3A-deficient cells.

claim: Most hyper-DMRA regions (~1200) remained hypomethylated across time in 3A-HET cells.
source: In fact, when we plotted the methylation of the hyper-DMRA in young and old 3A-HET cells, most of them (~1200) remained hypomethylated across time (Figure 8G, purple and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 8G and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DNMT3A is essential to modulate the DNA methylation landscape during adipocyte development and aging.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DNMT3A is essential to modulate the DNA methylation landscape during adipocyte development and aging, and that even heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a blunts these dynamics.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the DNA methylation dynamics data.

claim: Even heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a blunts DNA methylation dynamics during adipocyte development and aging.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that DNMT3A is essential to modulate the DNA methylation landscape during adipocyte development and aging, and that even heterozygous loss of Dnmt3a blunts these dynamics.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the DNA methylation dynamics data.

claim: Hypo-DMRA were largely associated with inflammatory and metabolic pathways.
source: Our analysis revealed that hypo-DMRA were largely associated with inflammatory and metabolic pathways, while hyper-DMRA were enriched for pathways associated with stem cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hyper-DMRA were enriched for pathways associated with stem cells.
source: Our analysis revealed that hypo-DMRA were largely associated with inflammatory and metabolic pathways, while hyper-DMRA were enriched for pathways associated with stem cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Lower DNA methylation in hypo-DMRA regions in young HET cells correlates with higher activation of pro-inflammatory trajectory B.
source: Because WT hypo-DMRA were associated with pro-inflammatory pathways, we hypothesized that lower DNA methylation in those regions in young HET cells would correlate with higher activation of pro-inflammatory trajectory B.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis tested by correlating DNA methylation with gene expression.

claim: Significant correlation was detected between hypo-DMRA and gene expression for 3A-HET primed pre-adipocytes, and weaker correlation for committed pre-adipocytes.
source: We detected significant correlation for the 3A-HET primed pre-adipocytes, and weaker correlation for committed pre-adipocytes (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Pro-inflammatory-associated regions that lose methylation during WT aging and are even less methylated in HET cells show increased gene expression in 3A-HET primed and committed cell clusters.
source: These results indicate that pro-inflammatory-associated regions that lose methylation during WT aging and are even less methylated in HET cells show increased gene expression in 3A-HET primed and committed cell clusters.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation between DNA methylation and gene expression.

claim: Reduced DNA methylation in hypo-DMRA regions permits the activation of pro-inflammatory genes.
source: Thus, reduced DNA methylation in those regions permits the activation of the pro-inflammatory genes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the relationship between DNA methylation and gene expression.

claim: Activation of Irf1, Socs3, and Jak2 in adipocytes has been previously associated with metabolic disease and inflammation.
source: Examples of genes with this behavior include Irf1, Socs3 and Jak2 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C). Activation of all these genes in adipocytes previously has been associated with metabolic disease and inflammation (Friesen et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature on these genes.

claim: WT-defined hyper-DMRAs are regions highly enriched for pathways associated with stem cell and pluripotency.
source: We found WT-defined hyper-DMRAs to be regions highly enriched for pathways associated with stem cell and pluripotency, suggesting that the stem cell program is repressed as WT adipose tissue ages and stem cells differentiate (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F (likely referring to Figure 9).

claim: The stem cell program is repressed as WT adipose tissue ages and stem cells differentiate.
source: We found WT-defined hyper-DMRAs to be regions highly enriched for pathways associated with stem cell and pluripotency, suggesting that the stem cell program is repressed as WT adipose tissue ages and stem cells differentiate (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the DNA methylation changes and pathway enrichment.

claim: HET cells displayed high correlation with activation of WT hyper-DMRA genes at one year of age.
source: Indeed, when we calculated the enrichment score of the gene expression profile from our scRNAseq of WT and HET at one year of age, HET cells displayed high correlation with activation of WT hyper-DMRA, which include known stromal progenitor genes such as F3, Krueppel-like factor 9 (Klf9), protein phosphatase 1 (Dusp1) and PDGF receptor β (Pdgfrb) (Figure 9C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 9C, D.

claim: F3 is known for its role as an inhibitory adipogenesis regulator.
source: Interestingly, F3 is known for its role in inhibitory adipogenesis regulators (Schwalie et al., 2018), suggesting inhibited differentiation in HET cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature on F3 function.

claim: The failure to gain DNA methylation with age in obese mice promotes enduring expression of stem and progenitor genes, consistent with faulty adipocytes.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the failure to gain DNA methylation with age in obese mice promotes enduring expression of stem and progenitor genes, consistent with faulty adipocytes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the combined DNA methylation and gene expression data.
